dedupe_keys.name: southeast louisiana veterans hospital rebuilt to withstand flooding after hurricane katrina

description: This case study from the U.S. Climate Resilience Toolkit describes how the Southeast Louisiana Veterans Health Care System replaced two New Orleans hospitals destroyed by flooding after Hurricane Katrina's levee failures with a new teaching hospital designed to keep operating if the levees fail again. Its contents are the climate stressors (flooding from storm surge and rainfall, a city partly below sea level, rising seas), the design response and its capacities. Mission-critical mechanical and electrical plant sits on upper floors, the so-called upside-down hospital; the emergency department and patient beds are at least 20 feet above the FEMA base flood elevation; an ambulance ramp doubles as a boat launch and the parking roof as a heliport; the energy plant stores 320,000 gallons of fuel for a week of independent operation; over a million gallons of rainwater can be stored; on-site sewage treatment holds waste for five to seven days; and the enclosure resists at least Category 3 hurricane winds. The toolkit, run by NOAA's Climate Program Office, published it in 2020 with links to the project's own pages. Coverage is one hospital campus in New Orleans. Access: a free, openly readable web page with references, links to project pages and related adaptation options. Caveats: it is a narrative case study, not a quantitative risk assessment, and the design facts are reported, not independently verified. Simulation uses: an example for climate adaptation, flood resilience and emergency response planning of hospitals as critical facilities. Related records: none catalogued yet; health facility inventories such as Healthsites.io (catalogued as data-healthsites-io) locate hospitals exposed to similar hazards.
